evidence.claim: An old stage-road alignment links the county seat and its schools.
evidence.quote: The western 11 miles (18 km) roughly follow the old Richmond-Williamsburg Stage Road

evidence.claim: An old stage-road alignment links the county seat and its schools.
evidence.quote: SR 249 passes through New Kent, which features the county courthouse, county offices, and the county's high school and middle school.

evidence.claim: New Kent Highway narrows from four divided lanes near I-64 to an undivided two-lane road as it curves east.
evidence.quote: SR 249 passes through the interchange as a four-lane divided highway but reduces to a two-lane undivided road as it curves east.

evidence.claim: It crosses a county of wooded and agricultural rolling hills, with the Pamunkey River defining the northeastern border and the Chickahominy the southwestern one.
evidence.quote: The northeastern border of the county is defined by the meanderings of the Pamunkey River, and the southwestern county border is similarly defined by the Chickahominy River. The county terrain consists of rolling hills, either wooded or devoted to agriculture, and carved by drainages.

evidence.claim: The western 11 miles of SR 249 roughly follow the Richmond-Williamsburg Stage Road, heavily used by Confederate and Union troops during the Peninsula Campaign in 1862.
evidence.quote: The western 11 miles (18 km) roughly follow the old Richmond-Williamsburg Stage Road, and it currently is named New Kent Highway. (The continuation east across SR 33 as State Route 632 is still named Old Stage Road.) The Old Stage Road was one of two routes heavily used by both Confederate and Union troops in 1862 during the Peninsula Campaign of the American Civil War.

evidence.claim: As I-64 was being built east of Richmond, nearby SR 33 carried heavy weekend traffic toward waterfront destinations in eastern Virginia and had a high accident rate.
evidence.quote: In the early 1970s, the new I-64 was under construction east of Richmond. Although primarily following the alignment of US 60 in this area, traffic relief for other roadways was also anticipated. Nearby, SR 33 between Eltham and Quinton in New Kent County had an extraordinarily high accident rate due to heavy weekend traffic to waterfront points in eastern Virginia.

evidence.claim: The SR 249 number came in the early 1970s, assigned to a former section of SR 33.
evidence.quote: The current SR 249 was assigned in the early 1970s to a portion of former State Route 33 in New Kent County.

evidence.claim: SR 33 was rerouted onto I-64, leaving its old alignment as northern New Kent County's main local highway.
evidence.quote: SR 249, which is the old alignment of SR 33 before that highway was rerouted onto I-64, is the main local highway of northern New Kent County

evidence.claim: Heading east, the highway passes Quinton and reaches the SR 106 roundabout at Talleysville.
evidence.quote: The state highway passes through the hamlet of Quinton and meets the northern end of SR 106 (Emmaus Church Road) at a roundabout in Talleysville.

evidence.claim: Beyond Carps Corner comes New Kent, with its courthouse and schools.
evidence.quote: East of Carps Corner, the site of the highway's junction with SR 155 (Courthouse Road), SR 249 passes through New Kent, which features the county courthouse, county offices, and the county's high school and middle school.

evidence.claim: SR 249 ends at Angelview Church, where SR 30 and SR 33 meet; SR 30 continues southeast toward Williamsburg.
evidence.quote: The state highway reaches its eastern terminus at a four-way intersection with SR 30 and SR 33 at Angelview Church. SR 33 passes through the intersection as Eltham Road. SR 30 heads east concurrently with SR 33 toward West Point and southeast along a continuation of New Kent Highway toward Williamsburg.

evidence.claim: At that final junction, SR 33 follows Eltham Road, with SR 30 joining it toward West Point; the southeast branch continues the New Kent Highway name.
evidence.quote: SR 33 passes through the intersection as Eltham Road. SR 30 heads east concurrently with SR 33 toward West Point and southeast along a continuation of New Kent Highway toward Williamsburg.

evidence.claim: Crump's Mill stands behind the dam of an L-shaped millpond near Talleysville, on private property.
evidence.quote:
The mill sits behind the dam
that creates the 16-acre millpond. The mill and millpond are both located on private property.

evidence.claim: Crump's Mill stands behind the dam of an L-shaped millpond near Talleysville, on private property.
evidence.quote: Crump's Mill and Millpond is a historic grist mill and mill pond located near Talleysville

evidence.claim: Damming South Branch in the early nineteenth century created the pond.
evidence.quote: The damming of South Branch in the early-19th century created a large millpond in the shape of the letter "L."

evidence.claim: The present mill dates to the 1870s.
evidence.quote: The mill is dated to the 1870s

evidence.claim: Its predecessor, built before 1818, burned in 1872; the replacement operated until 1955.
evidence.quote: It replaced a mill built before 1818 and destroyed by fire in 1872, and remained in operation until 1955.

evidence.claim: A rectangular, two-story frame building with a gable roof, it retains much of its milling machinery.
evidence.quote: is a simple rectangular two-story frame structure with a gable roof. Much of the mill machinery survives at Crump's Mill.

evidence.claim: Curved gable ends and a brick tower distinguish St. Peter's Church near Talleysville.
evidence.quote: The gable roof has curvilinear gable ends; segmental arches appear over the windows of the church and the open arches of the tower

evidence.claim: Curved gable ends and a brick tower distinguish St. Peter's Church near Talleysville.
evidence.quote: nearby but not in Talleysville, Virginia

evidence.claim: Construction began in 1701 and finished in 1703, supervised by vestryman Colonel Joseph Foster.
evidence.quote: Construction began in 1701 (at a cost of 146,000 weight of tobacco) and was complete by 1703. The steeple was erected 12 years later. The builder of nearby Foster's Castle, Colonel Joseph Foster, was a vestryman and supervised construction at St. Peter's Church.

evidence.claim: Its rector, Rev. David Mossom, married Martha Custis and George Washington in 1759, but the ceremony's location remains disputed between the church and White House Plantation.
evidence.quote: On January 6, 1759, the Rector of St. Peter's, Rev. David Mossom, united Martha Custis and Colonel George Washington in marriage. Debate ensues over the exact location of the marriage; some believe it occurred within the church while others believe it took place a few miles away at the White House Plantation on the Pamunkey River.

evidence.claim: Union soldiers later stabled horses in the pews and carved their names into the exterior brickwork.
evidence.quote: Union soldiers stabled their horses in the pews and carved their names in the brick exterior.

evidence.claim: Much of the building has since been restored or replaced.
evidence.quote: Much of the interior and exterior has been restored or replaced

evidence.claim: The tower's open arches, pyramidal roof and four original stuccoed brick urns are part of its exterior.
evidence.quote: The two-story brick tower is of Flemish bond with some glazing and has a pyramidal roof. The top of the tower is also decorated by four original stuccoed brick urns.

evidence.claim: The tower's open arches, pyramidal roof and four original stuccoed brick urns are part of its exterior.
evidence.quote: the open arches of the tower

evidence.claim: St. Peter's Church has curved gable ends and a brick tower topped with four stuccoed urns.
evidence.quote: The top of the tower is also decorated by four original stuccoed brick urns.

evidence.quote: The gable roof has curvilinear gable ends

evidence.claim: Before desegregation, New Kent High School served white students while George W. Watkins served African American students.
evidence.quote: Before desegregation, George Watkins was the county's African American-only high school, while New Kent School was the high school for whites.

evidence.claim: Dr. Calvin C. Green led the push for desegregation in Green v. County School Board.
evidence.quote: Dr. Calvin C. Green, who led the push for desegregation in Green v. County School Board.

evidence.claim: In 1968, the Supreme Court ruled that the county's freedom-of-choice plan failed to provide prompt, meaningful desegregation.
evidence.quote: In the landmark school desegregation case Green v. County School Board of New Kent County (1968), the United States Supreme Court ruled that New Kent County's freedom of choice plan failed to provide prompt and meaningful desegregation

evidence.claim: After the ruling, the school board adopted integration by grade level, consolidating elementary grades at Watkins and secondary grades at New Kent.
evidence.quote: The New Kent School Board changed to a plan that integrated by grade level, consolidating elementary grades at George W. Watkins Elementary School and secondary grades at New Kent High School.

evidence.claim: The two schools became a National Historic Landmark in 2001.
evidence.quote: The pair of schools was declared a National Historic Landmark in 2001.

evidence.claim: The former New Kent campus now serves Rappahannock Community College; the school district built a new high school south of it.
evidence.quote: The campus is now used as the New Kent campus of Rappahannock Community College. The New Kent County school district has since built a new high school south of the former school.
